title: CAV3RN Hides Cyberespionage C2 Behind Google Apps Script and Lets DNS Pick the Route
content_md: Project CAV3RN, a modular cyberespionage framework targeting organizations in Israel, has added a new command-and-control (C2) design that hides traffic behind Google Apps Script. The malware uses DNS A-record responses to decide whether each request should travel through a Google relay or directly to an attacker-controlled HTTPS server. The newly identified communication component, GoogleService.dll, is a 64-bit .NET 8 NativeAOT module. It works with a local DLL broker, allowing operators to load, manage, and upgrade framework components while the infected host remains active. This design gives CAV3RN a flexible and resilient architecture. Before it checks for commands or sends results, GoogleService.dll makes a DNS query to a subdomain under studiotikva[.]com . The query includes a random value, the malware’s current error state, and a hexadecimal version of the victim identifier. CAV3RN DNS-Routes Google C2 The DNS response does more than resolve a domain. Its final IP-address octet works as an instruction for the malware. A response ending in 120 can select either the Google Apps Script channel or direct HTTPS, depending on the previous failure state. A response ending in 130 usually selects direct HTTPS, while 140 forces an exception. Other values generally push the malware toward Google Apps Script.
